title: Finite free completed coefficient extension is ordinary derived scalar extension
statement:
Let $\ell$ be a prime, let $E\subset L$ be finite extensions of $\mathbf Q_\ell$ with valuation rings $\mathcal O_E\subset\mathcal O_L$ and uniformizers $t=\varpi_E$, $v=\varpi_L$ [def-weil-l-adic-coefficient-extension], and let $Y$ be any scheme. Work on its small pro-etale site [def-weil-pbc-proetale-site]. Write $R=\widehat{\mathcal O}_{E,Y}=\varprojlim_n(\mathcal O_E/t^n)_Y$ and $S=\widehat{\mathcal O}_{L,Y}=\varprojlim_m(\mathcal O_L/v^m)_Y$ for the completed coefficient sheaves [def-weil-completed-integral-coefficients], where $(-)_Y$ is the constant sheaf [def-weil-pbc-constant-sheaf]. The inclusions of valuation rings give a canonical map $R\to S$. The $R$-module sheaf $S$ is finite free of rank $[L:E]$.

For $T=R,S$, write $D(T)$ for the derived category of sheaves of $T$-modules [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category, def-weil-abstract-derived-category]. Let $K\in D(R)$ be derived $t$-complete [def-weil-derived-complete]. Form ordinary derived change of rings $K\otimes_R^L S$ [lem-pur-derived-change-of-rings]. The reductions $S\to(\mathcal O_L/v^m)_Y$ induce the canonical completion map
$$
 \chi_{L/E,K}:K\otimes_R^L S\longrightarrow
 R\varprojlim_m\operatorname{Res}^L_m\bigl(K\otimes_R^L(\mathcal O_L/v^m)_Y\bigr)
 =K\otimes_{\mathcal O_E}\mathcal O_L,
$$
Here $m\geq1$, $\operatorname{Res}^L_m$ is restriction of scalars along $S\to(\mathcal O_L/v^m)_Y$ [def-pc-sheaf-restrict-scalars], and $R\varprojlim$ denotes the strict-tower cone model specified in [def-weil-integral-scalar-extension], a derived limit [def-weil-derived-limit]. More explicitly, on a K-flat resolution $P\to K$ [def-pc-kflat-complex] the compatible quotient maps $P\otimes_R S\to\operatorname{Res}^L_m(P\otimes_R(\mathcal O_L/v^m)_Y)$ define a map to the product killed strictly by $1-s$; the induced map to $\operatorname{Cone}(1-s)[-1]$ has zero component in the shifted product. The map $\chi_{L/E,K}$ is the resulting morphism in $D(S)$, independent of the resolution. The last functor is exactly the strict-tower integral scalar extension of [def-weil-integral-scalar-extension], and the right side is interpreted as its derived-limit realization [lem-weil-integral-scalar-extension-well-defined]. This map is an isomorphism, natural in $K$, and $K\otimes_R^L S$ is derived $v$-complete. For $L=E$ it is the natural derived-completeness map $K\to R\varprojlim_n K\otimes_R^L(\mathcal O_E/t^n)_Y$, after the multiplication isomorphism $K\otimes_R^L R\cong K$.

source.place: Lemma 6.8.2(1), pp. 58-59 (completed coefficient sheaves); Definition 3.4.10 and Lemma 3.4.12, pp. 22-23 (completed tensor and derived completeness); Proposition 3.5.1, p. 24 (completion as derived inverse limit). The finite-free coefficient-extension comparison is a consequence of these constructions, not a verbatim numbered lemma. Reduction of completed constant coefficients is Stacks Tag 093M, sites-modules.tex, lemma-completion-flat.

proof.text: By uniqueness of extended absolute values, $\mathcal O_E=E\cap\mathcal O_L$ and $0<|t|_L<1$. The DVR decomposition in $\mathcal O_L$ gives $t=u v^e$ with $u$ a unit and $e\geq1$. Completeness of $E$ implies $\mathcal O_E\cong\varprojlim_n\mathcal O_E/t^n$: choose compatible lifts, whose successive differences lie in $t^n\mathcal O_E$, take their Cauchy limit in $E$, and use the closed unit ball to keep it in $\mathcal O_E$; injectivity follows from $|t|_E^n\to0$. Apply the finiteness-over-complete-ring theorem to $A=\mathcal O_E$, $I=(t)$, $M=\mathcal O_L$. Its separatedness hypothesis follows from $|t|_L<1$. Its finite-quotient hypothesis holds because $\mathcal O_L/t\mathcal O_L=\mathcal O_L/v^e\mathcal O_L$ is a finite set. Thus $\mathcal O_L$ is a finite torsion-free $\mathcal O_E$-module, hence free. Inverting $t$ gives $\mathcal O_L[1/t]=L$ (since $t=u v^e$), so its rank is $d=[L:E]$. Choose a basis $b_1,\ldots,b_d$.

source.place: Tag 031D (lemma-finite-over-complete-ring); DVR finite torsion-free freeness, with the coefficient data as in Bhatt--Scholze 6.8.1

proof.text: For each $n$, the chosen basis and its coordinate inverse give inverse $(\mathcal O_E/t^n)_Y$-module maps $(\mathcal O_E/t^n)_Y^{\oplus d}\leftrightarrows(\mathcal O_L/t^n\mathcal O_L)_Y$, commuting with quotient transitions. The same inverse equations hold after constant sheafification. Ordinary inverse limits may be taken over $m=en$: a compatible family at these indices extends uniquely to index $m$ by reduction from any $en\geq m$, independently of that choice. Taking limits of the basis maps gives $R^{\oplus d}\cong S$, with the prescribed $R$-action, proving finite freeness. Here constant sheafification preserves the finite biproduct equations: the constant-presheaf maps are inverse and additive, and exact abelian sheafification preserves finite sums. Limits are sectionwise. This also constructs the canonical ring map $R\to S$: its finite projections are those induced by the inclusions of valuation rings.

source.place: Lemma 6.8.2(1), pp. 58-59; finite-free coefficient argument in the first paragraph of the blueprint scalar-extension composition proof

proof.text: Apply the completed-constant-coefficient quotient theorem to $\mathcal O_E,(t)$ and to $\mathcal O_L,(v)$: $R/t^nR\cong(\mathcal O_E/t^n)_Y$ and $S/v^mS\cong(\mathcal O_L/v^m)_Y$, compatibly with all quotient maps. Its flatness over the discrete constant DVR sheaf also makes multiplication by $t$ on $R$, and by $v$ on $S$, injective: tensor the injective multiplication map of the DVR with its flat completed sheaf. On $S$, $t=u v^e$ is consequently injective too. Both valuation rings are Noetherian because they are DVRs. For the multiplication argument, constant abelian sheafification is exact, so the injective multiplication map remains injective before tensoring with the flat completion.

source.place: Tag 093M, lemma-completion-flat, applied to powers of the uniformizer; exact sheafification, Tag 03CN

proof.text: Choose a K-flat resolution $P\to K$ with flat terms. Put $Q=P\otimes_R S$. Derived change of rings says that $Q$ represents $K\otimes_R^L S$, and K-flat change of rings says that $Q$ is K-flat with flat terms over $S$. Work on the small skeleton in the larger universe fixed for the pro-etale site. For the strict quotient towers in the next steps, countable products of module sheaves are exact and sectionwise. Thus their termwise products represent derived products, and the cone of $1-s$, shifted by $-1$, computes the strict-tower derived limit. Denote this cone for $H\otimes_T T/a^nT$ by $C_{T,a}(H)$, and its quotient-map unit, with zero shifted-product component, by $\eta_{T,a}$. This notation will only be used for $(T,a,H)=(R,t,P),(S,t,Q),(S,v,Q)$. To check the unit in this identification, resolve a strict tower $X_\bullet$ by a K-injective tower $I_\bullet$, as in the strict-tower theorem. Module sheaves have enough injectives by the cited K-injective existence theorem (apply it to a sheaf in degree zero). The Roos-complex theorem identifies $\lim I_\bullet\to\operatorname{Cone}(1-s_I)[-1]$ by the explicit map $(0,\iota)$. Exact products identify the cone of $X_\bullet$ with that of $I_\bullet$ by a quasi-isomorphism. A strict compatible map from $H$ factors through $\lim I_\bullet$, and its composite is exactly the cone map $(0,c)$. Thus this comparison respects the specified unit, not merely the derived-limit object.

source.place: Tag 070M, lemma-difficulty-K-injectives, split product-cone argument, as generalized by lem-weil-derived-limit-roos-complex; K-injective existence: injectives.tex Tag 079P, theorem-K-injective-embedding-grothendieck

proof.text: For each of these three pairs $(T,a)$, regularity from step 3 implies that $[T\xrightarrow{a^n}T]$ in degrees $[-1,0]$ maps quasi-isomorphically to $T/a^nT$: its only possible extra cohomology is $\ker(a^n)=0$. The transitions $(a,1)$ commute with the quotient maps and the degree-zero units. Tensoring these maps with the K-flat $H$ preserves quasi-isomorphisms by its defining property. Exact products preserve the resulting levelwise quasi-isomorphisms, and taking their product cones therefore identifies the Koszul completion with $C_{T,a}(H)$, including its unit $\eta_{T,a}$. The cited Koszul reflector consequently says that $C_{T,a}(H)$ is locally derived $(a)$-complete and that this specified unit is invertible precisely when $H$ is locally derived $(a)$-complete. The only comparison here is the displayed two-term quotient quasi-isomorphism; no uniqueness of lifts in a triangulated category is used.

source.place: Tag 0A0E, lemma-derived-completion-koszul, and Tag 099B, lemma-derived-completion; regular one-generator Koszul quotient computed explicitly

proof.text: The hypothesis of derived $t$-completeness says that $K$ is a derived limit of its reduction tower through a Roos triangle with the prescribed reduction maps. By the completed-coefficient quotient isomorphisms of step 3 and the K-flat formula for integral reduction, this is the quotient tower of $P$. The object $C_{R,t}(P)$ is another derived limit of that tower; existence and uniqueness up to isomorphism of derived-limit objects give $K\cong C_{R,t}(P)$. Step 5 shows that the latter is locally derived $(t)$-complete. This local vanishing condition is invariant under isomorphism, so $K$ is locally derived $(t)$-complete. The unit criterion in step 5 now proves that the specified $\eta_{R,t}$ is an isomorphism. The noncanonical limit isomorphism was used only to establish a property of the object, never to identify a lift of its reduction map.

source.place: Lemma 3.4.12, pp. 22-23, and Definition 3.4.10; finite sums applied to the multiplication telescope

proof.text: The basis in step 2 identifies the underlying $R$-complex of $Q$ with $P^{\oplus d}$, and identifies its $t^n$ quotients and quotient maps with the finite sums of those of $P$. Sectionwise countable products commute with this finite sum, and the cone differential is the corresponding finite block sum. Thus the underlying $R$-map of $\eta_{S,t}:Q\to C_{S,t}(Q)$ is $\eta_{R,t}^{\oplus d}$ and is an isomorphism. The general module-sheaf forgetful theorem, clause (1), says that forgetting to abelian sheaves is faithful and preserves kernels and cokernels, for both $R$ and $S$. Restriction of scalars keeps precisely this underlying sheaf. It therefore preserves cohomology and detects its vanishing: an object with zero underlying sheaf has zero identity by faithfulness. Thus restriction detects acyclicity and detects isomorphisms of these derived maps. Hence $\eta_{S,t}$ is an isomorphism in $D(S)$. Apply the Koszul reflector for $S,t$, whose regularity was checked in step 3; its unit criterion shows that $Q$ is locally derived $(t)$-complete as an $S$-object.

source.place: Lemma 3.4.12, pp. 22-23, and Definition 3.4.10; finite sums applied to the multiplication telescope

proof.text: The one-generator augmented extended Cech complexes for $S,t$ and $S,v$ are respectively $[S\to S[1/t]]$ and $[S\to S[1/v]]$, in degrees $[0,1]$, with augmentation to $S$ the degree-zero identity. They are canonically identical: $t=u v^e$ gives $1/t=u^{-1}/v^e$ and $1/v=u v^{e-1}/t$, defining inverse localization maps which fix $S$. The extended-Cech completion theorem identifies the derived internal Hom from these augmented complexes as the corresponding reflection units. Since $Q$ is locally $(t)$-complete, its first reflection unit is an isomorphism; the identical augmented complexes give an isomorphism for the $(v)$ reflection unit. Its value is locally $(v)$-complete, so $Q$ itself is locally $(v)$-complete. The Koszul reflector for $S,v$ now gives an isomorphism of its specified quotient completion unit $\eta_v:Q\to C_{S,v}(Q)$, by the regular Koszul-to-quotient comparison in step 5. Its cone triangle and this unit exhibit the Roos completeness condition for $Q$.

source.place: Tag 099B, lemma-derived-completion, augmented localization model; Tag 0A0E, lemma-derived-completion-koszul

proof.text: Identify that quotient tower termwise: $(P\otimes_R S)\otimes_S S/v^mS\to P\otimes_R(\mathcal O_L/v^m)_Y$ sends $(p\otimes s)\otimes\bar z$ to $p\otimes\overline{s}z$, with inverse $p\otimes\bar z\mapsto(p\otimes1)\otimes\bar z$. These inverse formulas commute with the differential and quotient transitions and send the map from $Q$ to its original coefficient-reduction map. Therefore the isomorphism of the two product cones carries $\eta_v$ to exactly $\chi_{L/E,K}$, including its zero shifted-product component. The scalar-extension well-definedness theorem identifies this cone with the stated integral functor and its derived-limit realization. This proves all isomorphism and derived $v$-completeness claims.

source.place: Definition 3.4.10, Lemma 3.4.12 and Proposition 3.5.1; the quotient maps identify the strict integral-extension cone

proof.text: For a map of K-flat representatives $f:P\to P'$, each quotient square commutes because both routes send $p\otimes s$ to $f(p)\otimes\overline{s}$. The product squares commute with $1-s$, so the induced cone square gives $\chi_{K'}(f\otimes1)=R\lim_m(f\otimes1)\chi_K$. The derived change-of-rings and integral-extension well-definedness statements, and naturality of the Koszul reflector unit, carry this equality to all morphisms of the derived category: the resolving-class construction localizes the K-flat subcategory at quasi-isomorphisms, and the square remains commutative after inverting such a map, hence for every composite of maps and inverse quasi-isomorphisms. The same descent proves independence of the representative for the specified cone map. No basis enters the definition of $\chi$. When $L=E$ take the same uniformizer; the inverse multiplication maps $P\otimes_R R\leftrightarrows P$ identify every quotient square with the reduction of $P$. Thus $\chi$ is precisely the canonical completeness unit. For different choices of a uniformizer of the same field the powers define the same ideals and the same quotient maps, giving the same conclusion.
